Calculate Governance Scores

Source: R/get-scores.R
get_scores.Rd

Scores organizations on the nonprofit governance index. By default (model = "2023") the function returns the 2023 governance index, an item response score on a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation 15 among all 501(c)(3) full Form 990 filers in tax year 2023, together with the scores from the 2023 bifactor measurement model and a simple count of practices. The original 2018 six-factor model remains available as model = "legacy-2018".

Usage

get_scores(
  feature.matrix,
  model = c("2023", "legacy-2018"),
  missing = TRUE,
  impute = "median",
  scores.by.hand = FALSE
)

Arguments

feature.matrix

A data.frame of features, the output of get_features. For model = "2023" it must contain the 16 GI_* item columns; for model = "legacy-2018" the 12 legacy features ("P12_LINE_1", "P4_LINE_12", ...).

model

Which scoring model to apply: "2023" (default) or "legacy-2018".

missing, impute, scores.by.hand

Used only by model = "legacy-2018"; passed to psych::factor.scores as in earlier versions. With missing = FALSE, rows with NA features are dropped.

Value

The input data frame with appended columns.

For model = "2023":

gov_score

The governance index: mean 100 and SD 15 among 2023 501(c)(3) full-990 filers, so 115 is one standard deviation above the average 2023 filer. It ranges from about 67 (none of the 16 practices) to about 128 (all 16), and adding a practice never lowers it.

gov_score_se

Standard error of gov_score, in index points (about 4 in the middle of the distribution, about 10 at the extremes).

gov_score_bf

General factor of the 2023 bifactor model (latent scale, 2023 mean 0). This was gov_score in version 0.1.0. It correlates .99 with the index but can fall when a practice is added, so it is not recommended as a published score.

gov_s_finance, gov_s_minutes, gov_s_policy, gov_s_comp

Specific-factor scores of the bifactor model for financial assurance, meeting minutes, written policies, and compensation process. These are residual dimensions, orthogonal to gov_score_bf: a positive value means the organization does more in that area than its general level predicts. They are not standalone subscales, and they are much less reliable than the index (empirical reliability among 2023 filers: finance .57, compensation .48, minutes .41, policy .29). Only gov_s_finance carries substantial variance of its own. Do not use gov_s_policy: the written-policy items are the core of the general factor, and the policy factor has almost no variance of its own (omega-hierarchical < .01); it only contrasts the conflict-of-interest items with the whistleblower and retention policies. It is returned for completeness.

gov_count

Number of the 16 practices present (0–16), a transparent alternative that correlates about .96 with gov_score.

gov_n_items

Number of the 16 items answered. Rows with no answered items get NA scores.

For model = "legacy-2018": six factor scores and total.score, as in earlier versions of the package.

Details

The index (gov_score). The index is the expected a posteriori (EAP) estimate from a unidimensional graded response model (gov_index_2023). Nested practices are scored as ordinal items:

  • financial assurance: compiled or reviewed, audited, audited with an audit committee (0–3);

  • conflict-of-interest policy: policy, annual disclosure, monitoring (0–3);

  • minutes: board and committee minutes (0–2);

  • pay-setting process: CEO and other officers (0–2);

and accrual accounting, a majority-independent board, Form 990 review by the board, whistleblower and document retention policies, and posting the 990 online are binary items. Because the model has one dimension and positive slopes, an organization's index can only rise when it reports another practice. Its value is 100 + 15 * (theta - mu) / sd, where mu and sd are the mean and standard deviation of the 2023 estimates. Item parameters and both constants are fixed at their 2023 values, so the index for other tax years is on the 2023 scale; the items show no meaningful differential functioning across tax years 2021–2024. Missing items are handled by the model (scores use the answered items).

How much a practice adds depends on which practice it is and where an organization starts: in 2023 the written policies added 7 to 12 points on average and most other practices 1 to 4. See vignette("making-gov-scores", package = "governance") for the points per practice, interpretation, and limitations, including the ceiling at about 128.

Bifactor scores. gov_score_bf and the gov_s_* columns come from the 2023 bifactor model (gov_model_2023), a general factor plus four testlets (financial assurance; minutes; written policies; compensation). It describes how the items covary better than the index model does and supports a single score, but its EAP estimates are not monotone in the items (Hooker, Finkelman and Schwartzman 2009): in 2023 data, adding committee minutes lowered gov_score_bf for most organizations that lacked them.

Three financial-assurance items (audit, review or audit, accrual) show moderate differential item functioning by organization size: at the same general level, larger organizations are more likely to be audited, in part because of legal and funder audit thresholds. Keep this in mind when comparing organizations of very different size.

Legacy model. The 2018 model has known problems, including negative implied weights on several good-practice features and a training sample that excluded fully independent boards. It is kept for reproducing earlier work. See "Known issues" in vignette("legacy-2018-model", package = "governance").

References

Hooker, G., Finkelman, M., and Schwartzman, A. (2009). Paradoxical results in multidimensional item response theory. Psychometrika, 74(3), 419–442.

See also

get_features, gov_index_2023, gov_model_2023.

Examples

data("dat_example", package = "governance")
set.seed(57)
dat_example <- dat_example[sample(seq_len(nrow(dat_example)), 200), ]
features_example <- get_features(dat_example)

# 2023 index (default)
scores_example <- get_scores(features_example)
summary(scores_example$gov_score)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   67.33   87.76   99.56  100.05  111.34  128.29 

# legacy 2018 model
legacy <- get_scores(features_example, model = "legacy-2018")
